attempts.raw_response: Thus, while they strip the creature of all understanding, they are constrained to clothe the Creator with it in the highest degree. The more they depress the animal, the more they exalt the divine artifice, since a machine that moves with such exactness and performs so many admirable operations without thought, must have been framed by an intelligence infinitely superior to what the most sagacious beast could possibly possess. In denying reason to the work, they ascribe it more eminently to the workman; and the very argument they use to degrade the brute creation turns into a new proof of the inexhaustible wisdom that contrived and disposed the whole. So that, upon the whole, their hypothesis, though intended to lessen the dignity of animals, does but establish more firmly the glory of the supreme Architect.

pair.human_continuation:
Thus the most
opposite philosophers perfectly agree in acknowledging that matter
and chance cannot, without the help of art, produce all we observe
in animals.


SECT.  IX.  A Particular Examination of Nature.


After these comparisons, about which I only desire the reader to
consult himself, without any argumentation, I think it is high time
to enter into a detail of Nature.  I do not pretend to penetrate
through the whole; who is able to do it?  Neither do I pretend to
enter into any physical discussion.  Such way of reasoning requires
a certain deep knowledge, which abundance of men of wit and sense
never acquired; and, therefore, I will offer nothing to them but the
simple prospect of the face of Nature.
pair.prefix:
Hence it appears that sound reason naturally
concludes that matter alone cannot, either by the simple laws of
motion, or by the capricious strokes of chance, make even animals
that are mere machines.  Those philosophers themselves, who will not
allow beasts to have any reasoning faculty, cannot avoid
acknowledging that what they suppose to be blind and artless in
these machines is yet full of wisdom and art in the First Mover, who
made their springs and regulated their movements.

source_document.title: The Existence of God by Francois de Salignac de La Mothe-Fenelon
